questions.title: Relational database
questions.text: Describe what is meant by a **relational database**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Data is stored in several tables (relations), each about one entity (1)
- the tables are linked by keys — a primary key in one table is a foreign key in another (1)
scheme.model_answer: A database that stores data in several tables, each about one entity, which are linked to each other using primary and foreign keys.

questions.title: Advantage of a relational database
questions.text: State **one** advantage of using a relational database.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any one (1): reduced data redundancy / less repeated data; maintains data consistency / improves data integrity; changes in one table are automatically reflected; less storage; complex queries across tables; better security / sharing
scheme.model_answer: It reduces data redundancy, because each item of data is stored only once.

questions.title: Problems of a flat file
questions.text:
| LoanID | Student | Class | Book |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Aruzhan Bekova | 11A | The Hobbit |
| 2 | Aruzhan Bekova | 11A | Abai Zholy |
| 3 | Aruzhan Bekova | 11A | Dune |

A library stores loans in this single table. Explain **one** problem this causes when Aruzhan moves to class 11B.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Aruzhan's class is stored in every row / data redundancy (1)
- every row must be updated; if one is missed the data becomes inconsistent (update anomaly) (1)
scheme.model_answer: Her class is stored in all three rows, so all of them must be changed; if one is missed, the table shows two different classes for her and becomes inconsistent.

questions.title: Flat file or relational
questions.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show whether the statement describes a **flat-file** or a **relational** database.

prefill: All the data is held in one table
Tables are linked using primary and foreign keys
The same data is often repeated in many records
Each fact is stored only once

scheme.mark_scheme:
1 Flat; 2 Relational; 3 Flat; 4 Relational

Four correct (3); three (2); two (1)
scheme.ai_instructions: Award 3 for four correct rows, 2 for three, 1 for two.

questions.title: Database terms
questions.text: Match each term to its definition.

right.text: A collection of related fields about one item
One item of data stored about every record
A sorted structure with pointers that speeds up searching

scheme.mark_scheme: Table–R1, Record–R2, Field–R3, Index–R4. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: Other names
questions.text:
Complete the sentences.

In relational database terms, a row of a table is called a [[1]], a column is called an [[2]] and a table is called a [[3]].

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) tuple / record (2) attribute / field (3) relation

questions.title: Define record and table
questions.text: Define the terms **record** and **table**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Record: a collection of related fields (about one item / entity) (1)
Table: a collection of related records (1)
scheme.model_answer: Record: a collection of related fields about one item. Table: a collection of related records.

questions.title: Choose data types
questions.text: Complete the table with the most suitable **data type** for each field. Use: **text**, **integer**, **real**, **date**, **Boolean**.

scheme.mark_scheme: PhoneNumber – text (1); Price – real (1); DateOfBirth – date (1); HasPaid – Boolean (1)

questions.title: Why a phone number is text
questions.text: Explain why a phone number such as `+7 701 123 45 67` should be stored with the **text** data type rather than as an integer.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): it contains + / spaces which are not digits; a leading 0 would be lost as a number; no calculations are performed on phone numbers; it may be too long for an integer
scheme.model_answer: It contains characters such as + and spaces that an integer cannot store, and no calculations are ever done on phone numbers.

questions.title: Purpose of an index
questions.text: Describe the purpose of an **index** in a database.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Stores the values of a field in sorted order with pointers to the records (1)
- so records can be found / searched / sorted faster without reading the whole table (1)
scheme.model_answer: An index keeps the values of a field in sorted order with pointers to the records, so the DBMS can find matching records quickly instead of reading the whole table.

questions.title: Indexes and updates
questions.text: Adding an index to a field makes inserting and updating records faster.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: An index speeds up searching, but every insert or update must also update the index, so these operations become slower.

questions.title: Primary key
questions.text: Define the term **primary key**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- A field / combination of fields that uniquely identifies each record in a table (1)
- cannot be empty or repeated (1)
scheme.model_answer: A field whose value uniquely identifies each record in a table; it cannot be repeated or left empty.

questions.title: Identify the keys
questions.text:
```text
Customers ( CustomerID, Name, City )
Products  ( ProductID, Name, Price )
Orders    ( OrderID, CustomerID, ProductID, OrderDate )
```

Complete the table to show the primary key and the foreign key(s) of each table. For a table with no foreign key, write **None**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Customers – CustomerID – None (1)
Products – ProductID – None (1)
Orders – OrderID – CustomerID, ProductID (1)
1 mark for each correct row.

rows: CustomerID, ProductID||ProductID, CustomerID||CustomerID and ProductID||ProductID and CustomerID||CustomerID,ProductID||ProductID,CustomerID

questions.title: Primary vs foreign key
questions.text: Using the tables `Customers(CustomerID, Name, City)` and `Orders(OrderID, CustomerID, OrderDate)`, explain the difference between a primary key and a foreign key.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- CustomerID is the primary key of Customers: it uniquely identifies each customer (1)
- CustomerID in Orders is a foreign key: it links each order to the customer who placed it (can be repeated) (1)

points.criterion: Primary key uniquely identifies, with example
Foreign key links tables, with example

scheme.model_answer: CustomerID uniquely identifies each customer in the Customers table, so it is the primary key there. In Orders, CustomerID is a foreign key that links each order to the customer who made it, and it can appear many times.

questions.title: Composite key
questions.text: In the table `Results(StudentID, SubjectID, Mark)` each student has a mark for many subjects. Which is the best primary key?

scheme.mark_scheme: D
scheme.explanation: Neither field is unique on its own, but each pair (student, subject) appears only once — a composite key.

questions.title: Simple vs composite keys
questions.text: State the difference between **simple** and **composite** primary keys.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Simple primary keys use a single field… (1)
… composite primary keys use multiple fields (1)
scheme.model_answer: A simple primary key is one field, whereas a composite primary key is made of two or more fields that together are unique.

questions.title: Foreign key values
questions.text: The same foreign-key value can appear in many records of a table.

scheme.mark_scheme: True.
scheme.explanation: One customer can have many orders, so the same CustomerID appears in many Orders records.

questions.title: Referential integrity
questions.text: Explain what is meant by **referential integrity**, using the `Customers` and `Orders` tables as an example.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Every foreign-key value must match an existing primary-key value in the linked table (1)
- e.g. an order cannot be added for a CustomerID that does not exist in Customers / a customer with orders cannot be deleted (1)
scheme.model_answer: Every foreign key value must refer to an existing record: an order cannot contain CustomerID C999 if there is no customer C999 in the Customers table.

questions.title: A school database
questions.text:
```text
Teachers ( TeacherID, Name, Subject )
Classes  ( ClassID, Room, TeacherID )
Pupils   ( PupilID, Name, DateOfBirth, ClassID )
```

parts.title: Foreign keys
parts.text: Identify the foreign key in the `Classes` table and in the `Pupils` table.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Classes: TeacherID (1)
Pupils: ClassID (1)
scheme.model_answer: Classes: TeacherID. Pupils: ClassID.

parts.title: Why not Name
parts.text: Explain why `Name` is **not** a suitable primary key for the `Pupils` table.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Two pupils can have the same name / names are not unique (1)
- so Name would not uniquely identify each record / names can change (1)
scheme.model_answer: Two pupils may have the same name, so Name would not uniquely identify each pupil's record.

parts.title: Field and record
parts.text: Give an example of a **field** and describe what one **record** in the `Pupils` table contains.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Field (1): PupilID / Name / DateOfBirth / ClassID
Record (1): all the data (PupilID, Name, DateOfBirth, ClassID) about one pupil
scheme.model_answer: Field: DateOfBirth. Record: the ID, name, date of birth and class of one pupil.

questions.title: Explain a relational design
questions.text:
A gym stores all its data in one table:

`Visits(MemberName, MemberPhone, TrainerName, TrainerPhone, VisitDate)`

Explain why a relational database would be better, and describe a relational design with suitable tables, primary keys and foreign keys.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Why better (max 3): member / trainer details repeated in every visit — redundancy (1); update anomalies / inconsistency when a phone number changes (1); wasted storage (1); no unique identifier — names not unique (1)
Design (max 3): Members(MemberID, Name, Phone) (1); Trainers(TrainerID, Name, Phone) (1); Visits(VisitID, MemberID*, TrainerID*, VisitDate) with foreign keys identified (1)

points.criterion: Visits table with both foreign keys

scheme.model_answer: In the single table, a member's name and phone and the trainer's details are repeated for every visit, which wastes space; if a phone number changes, every row must be updated or the data becomes inconsistent, and names are not unique identifiers. A better design: Members(MemberID, Name, Phone) with primary key MemberID; Trainers(TrainerID, Name, Phone) with primary key TrainerID; Visits(VisitID, MemberID, TrainerID, VisitDate) with primary key VisitID and foreign keys MemberID and TrainerID linking each visit to a member and a trainer.

questions.title: A clinic database
questions.text:
A clinic uses a relational database with three tables.

```text
Patients     ( PatientID, Name, DateOfBirth, Phone )
Doctors      ( DoctorID, Name, Speciality )
Appointments ( AppointmentID, PatientID, DoctorID, AppDate, AppTime )
```

parts.title: Keys
parts.text: Complete the following table to show for each database table the primary key and the foreign key(s). For a table with no foreign key, write **None**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Patients – PatientID – None (1)
Doctors – DoctorID – None (1)
Appointments – AppointmentID – PatientID, DoctorID (1)
1 mark for each correct row.

rows: PatientID, DoctorID||DoctorID, PatientID||PatientID and DoctorID||DoctorID and PatientID||PatientID,DoctorID||DoctorID,PatientID

scheme.mark_scheme:
A record is a collection of related fields (1)
A table is a collection of related records (1)
scheme.model_answer: Record: a collection of related fields. Table: a collection of related records.

parts.title: Primary and foreign keys
parts.text: Explain the differences of using primary and foreign keys in the given database.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- A primary key (e.g. PatientID) uniquely identifies each record in its table (Patients) (1)
- A foreign key (e.g. PatientID in Appointments) links a record to the related record in another table (1)
Accept answers only with fields from the given database.
scheme.model_answer: PatientID uniquely identifies each patient in the Patients table, so it is the primary key; in Appointments, PatientID is a foreign key that links each appointment to the patient.

parts.title: Data types
parts.text: State the most suitable data type for the fields `DateOfBirth` and `Phone`.

scheme.mark_scheme:
DateOfBirth: Date (1)
Phone: Text / String / VARCHAR (1)
scheme.model_answer: DateOfBirth: date. Phone: text.

parts.title: Advantage
parts.text: State **one** advantage of using a relational database for the clinic.

scheme.mark_scheme: Reduced data redundancy / less repeated data (1); maintains data consistency / improves data integrity (1); changes in one table automatically reflected (1) [Max 1]
scheme.model_answer: Each patient's details are stored only once, so there is less repeated data.

questions.title: Exam results
questions.text:
A school stores exam results in the table `Results ( StudentID, SubjectID, Mark )`.

| StudentID | SubjectID | Mark |
|---|---|---|
| S01 | MATH | 78 |
| S01 | PHYS | 65 |
| S02 | MATH | 91 |

parts.title: Why not StudentID
parts.text: Explain why `StudentID` on its own cannot be the primary key of `Results`.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- StudentID is repeated (S01 appears twice) because a student has results in several subjects (1)
- a primary key must be unique for every record (1)
scheme.model_answer: S01 appears in two records because one student has marks in several subjects, but a primary key must be different for every record.

parts.title: Composite key
parts.text: Identify the field(s) that can be used as the primary key for `Results`.

scheme.mark_scheme: StudentID and SubjectID (together) (1). Do not award the mark if only one field is given.
scheme.model_answer: StudentID and SubjectID together.

parts.title: Simple vs composite
parts.text: State the difference between simple and composite primary keys.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Simple primary keys use a single field… (1)
… composite primary keys use multiple fields (1)
scheme.model_answer: A simple key is one field; a composite key uses two or more fields together.

scheme.mark_scheme: A tuple is one row / record in a database (table) (1)
scheme.model_answer: One row (record) of a table.

parts.title: Foreign key
parts.text: The school also has a table `Students ( StudentID, Name, Class )`. Explain how `StudentID` links the two tables.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- StudentID is the primary key of Students (1)
- and a foreign key in Results, so each result is linked to the student it belongs to (1)
scheme.model_answer: StudentID is the primary key of Students and appears in Results as a foreign key, so each result can be matched to the student it belongs to.

parts.title: Referential integrity
parts.text: Explain why the DBMS should not allow a result with `StudentID = S99` to be entered if there is no student S99 in `Students`.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Referential integrity: every foreign-key value must match an existing primary key (1)
- otherwise the result belongs to no student / data is inconsistent / invalid links (1)
scheme.model_answer: Referential integrity requires every foreign key to match an existing primary key; a result for S99 would not belong to any real student, so the data would be invalid.

questions.title: A shop's sales table
questions.text:
A small shop records all its sales in one table.

| SaleID | CustomerName | CustomerPhone | Product | Price |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Dana Seitova | 87011112233 | Notebook | 450 |
| 2 | Dana Seitova | 87011112233 | Pen | 150 |
| 3 | Arman Nurov | 87775554411 | Notebook | 450 |

parts.title: Redundancy
parts.text: Explain **one** problem caused by storing the data in this single table.

scheme.mark_scheme: Problem (1) + explanation (1): data redundancy — customer / product details repeated; update problems — if Dana's phone changes every row must change, or data becomes inconsistent; wasted storage
scheme.model_answer: Dana's name and phone number are repeated for every sale, so if her phone changes, every row must be updated; missing one makes the data inconsistent.

parts.title: Relational design
parts.text: Describe how the data could be stored in a relational database with **three** tables. Identify the primary key of each table.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Customers(CustomerID, Name, Phone) — PK CustomerID (1)
Products(ProductID, Name, Price) — PK ProductID (1)
Sales(SaleID, CustomerID, ProductID) — PK SaleID with foreign keys (1)
scheme.model_answer: Customers(CustomerID, Name, Phone) with primary key CustomerID; Products(ProductID, Name, Price) with primary key ProductID; Sales(SaleID, CustomerID, ProductID) with primary key SaleID and foreign keys CustomerID and ProductID.

parts.title: Index
parts.text: The shop often searches for sales by `CustomerID`. Describe how an **index** on this field would help.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- The index stores CustomerID values in sorted order with pointers to the records (1)
- so the sales for a customer are found quickly without reading the whole table (1)
scheme.model_answer: The index keeps the CustomerID values sorted with pointers to the matching sales, so the DBMS finds a customer's sales quickly instead of reading every record.

parts.title: Index drawback
parts.text: State **one** disadvantage of adding an index.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any one (1): uses extra storage; inserting / updating / deleting records is slower
scheme.model_answer: Adding new sales is slower because the index must be updated too.

parts.title: DBMS
parts.text: Describe the purpose of a database management system (DBMS).

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): software used to create / manage the database; allows data to be added, updated, deleted and searched / queried; controls access / security; enforces integrity / keys; allows many users to share data; backup and recovery
scheme.model_answer: A DBMS is software that creates and manages the database: it lets users add, update and search data, and controls who can access it.

summary: What a relational database is and why it is used, the terms table, record (tuple), field (attribute), data type and index, and the difference between primary, foreign and composite keys.

blocks.content: An **organised, structured collection of related data**, stored electronically so that it can be **searched, sorted, updated and analysed** easily. A **database management system (DBMS)** is the software used to create, manage and access the database (e.g. MySQL, PostgreSQL, Microsoft Access, SQLite).

A database in which the data is stored in **several linked tables** (relations). Each table holds data about **one type of thing (entity)**, and tables are **linked by keys** — a **primary key** in one table appears as a **foreign key** in another.

blocks.title: Flat-file database vs relational database
rows: Data split into **several tables** linked by keys
**High** — the same data (e.g. a teacher's name) is repeated in many rows
Copies can disagree after an update (**update anomaly**)
A change is made in **one place** and applies everywhere

blocks.title: Why split the data? A school library
blocks.content:
**Flat file:**
| LoanID | Student | Class | Book | Author |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Aruzhan Bekova | 11A | The Hobbit | J. R. R. Tolkien |
| 2 | Aruzhan Bekova | 11A | Abai Zholy | M. Auezov |
| 3 | Timur Ospanov | 12B | The Hobbit | J. R. R. Tolkien |

Aruzhan's class and *The Hobbit*'s author are stored **twice**. If Aruzhan moves to 11B, **every** row must be changed — miss one and the data becomes **inconsistent**.

**Relational:** a `Students` table, a `Books` table and a `Loans` table that only stores `StudentID`, `BookID` and the date — each student and each book is stored **once**.

items.title: Purpose / advantages of a relational database
items.content:
- **Reduced data redundancy** — less repeated data, less storage.
- **Data consistency and integrity** — a change in one table is seen everywhere; keys stop invalid links.
- **Easier updates** — data is changed in one place.
- **Powerful searching** — complex queries combine data from several tables.
- **Security** — users can be given access only to certain tables.
- **Data sharing** — many users and programs use the same data at the same time.

items.title: Typical uses
items.content:
- School information systems (students, classes, marks).
- Online shops (customers, products, orders).
- Banks, hospitals, libraries, airline bookings.
- The data behind almost every website and mobile app.

blocks.title: Database terms
rows: A thing about which data is stored
A **collection of related records** about one entity
A **collection of related fields** about **one** item
**One item of data** about every record
The data in one field of one record
The kind of data a field holds

blocks.content:
fields / attributes (columns)
                 +-----------+-----------+----------+--------+
                 | StudentID | FirstName | Surname  | Class  |
                 +-----------+-----------+----------+--------+
 record / tuple  | S001      | Aruzhan   | Bekova   | 11A    |   <- one row
 (rows)          | S002      | Timur     | Ospanov  | 12B    |
                 | S003      | Dana      | Seitova  | 11A    |

                   primary key
blocks.caption: The parts of a table

blocks.content: Store phone numbers, ID numbers and postcodes as **text**: you never do arithmetic on them, and they may start with `0` or `+`.

A separate data structure that stores the values of **one or more fields** in **sorted order** together with **pointers to the records**, so that the DBMS can **find records quickly** without reading the whole table — like the index at the back of a book.

items.title: Advantages of an index
items.content:
- **Searching and sorting are much faster**, especially in large tables.
- Speeds up **queries** that use `WHERE` and `JOIN` on the indexed field.
- A **unique index** prevents duplicate values (the primary key is indexed automatically).

items.title: Disadvantages
items.content:
- Takes **extra storage space**.
- **Inserting, updating and deleting** records is slower, because the index must also be updated.
- Too many indexes on small tables give little benefit.

blocks.title: When to add an index
blocks.content: A library table has 2 000 000 loans and staff often search by `StudentID` → add an index on `StudentID`. The `Notes` field is rarely searched → no index needed.
A field (or combination of fields) whose value **uniquely identifies each record** in a table. It **cannot be empty (null)** and **cannot be repeated**. Example: `StudentID` in `Students`.
A field in one table that is the **primary key of another table**. It is used to **link (relate)** the two tables. Example: `StudentID` in the `Loans` table links each loan to a student.

A primary key made of **two or more fields** that **together** uniquely identify a record, when no single field is unique on its own. Example: in `Results(StudentID, SubjectID, Mark)`, a student has many results and a subject has many results, but the pair **(StudentID, SubjectID)** is unique.

Students ( _StudentID_, FirstName, Surname, Class )
Books    ( _BookID_, Title, Author, Year )
Loans    ( _LoanID_, StudentID*, BookID*, LoanDate, ReturnDate )
blocks.caption: A relational database for a library (primary keys underlined with _, foreign keys marked *)

blocks.title: Primary key vs foreign key
rows: **Uniquely identifies** each record in **its own** table
**Links** a record to a record in **another** table
No — the same value can appear many times (one student has many loans)
Can be empty if the link is optional

blocks.title: Simple vs composite primary key
rows: A single field is always unique
No single field is unique on its own

blocks.title: Other kinds of key
blocks.content:
- **Candidate key** — any field that **could** be the primary key (e.g. `StudentID` or `PassportNo`).
- **Secondary (alternate) key** — a field that is **indexed** for searching but is not the primary key, e.g. `Surname`.

A rule enforced by the DBMS: every **foreign-key value must match an existing primary-key value** in the linked table. You cannot add a loan for student `S999` if no such student exists, and you cannot delete a student who still has loans (or the loans are deleted too).

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Define the terms record and table. [2]**
A **record** is a collection of related fields (about one item) (1). A **table** is a collection of related records (1).

**Q: Define the term tuple. [1]**
A tuple is **one row / record** in a database table.

**Q: State the difference between simple and composite primary keys. [2]**
Simple primary keys use a **single field** (1); composite primary keys use **multiple fields** (1).

**Q: Explain the difference between primary and foreign keys in the given database. [2]**
The primary key `pub_ID` **uniquely identifies each record** in the `Publishers` table (1); `pub_ID` in the `Titles` table is a **foreign key** that **links** each title to its publisher (1).

**Q: State one advantage of using a relational database. [1]**
**Reduced data redundancy** / less repeated data; or maintains **data consistency / integrity**; or a change in one table is automatically reflected everywhere.

- Mixing up **record** (a row) and **field** (a column).
- Saying the foreign key is unique — it is the **primary** key that is unique.
- Choosing a primary key that can repeat or be empty (e.g. `Surname`, `Class`).
- Giving only **one** field when the question asks for a composite key or for "all foreign keys".
- Saying an index makes **everything** faster — it slows down inserts and updates.
